For example, increasing demand for n-type solar cells has prompted a higher demand for silver due to these cells’ typically higher silver content (Zuboy et al. 2023). In other instances, material availability directly influences technological trends. For example, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) experts note that the amount of cobalt in nickel-manganese cobalt-oxide Li-ion battery cathodes has significantly dropped during the past decade in part to help reduce cobalt-related supply chain issues. 5.3 Other Unknowns New technologies often introduce unforeseen vulnerabilities that become apparent only after widespread adoption. For example,only after the widespread implementation of nuclear power did risks become clear: early assumptions held that technological advancements would enable safe storage or reprocessing of nuclear waste, but finding acceptable long-term storage solutions proved more complex than anticipated. Additionally, the risks of long-term health impacts from radiation exposure became more apparent after the 1986 Chernobyl and the 2011 Fukushima disasters. On a smaller scale, after the early adoption of energy-efficient light-emitting diode (LED) lighting, the U.S. Air Force issued a temporary moratorium on purchasing LED lighting until reliability issues were resolved, at which time the moratorium was lifted. 18 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 6 Risk Mitigation Strategies A number of mitigation options could help reduce vulnerabilities or potential consequences associated with the identified risk drivers. DOW is already pursuing many of these mitigations, but additional measures would enable DOW to increase resilience during times of conflict. The following mitigations could be integrated across DOW, prioritized within strategic initiatives, and informed by lessons learned from current DOW efforts. Where feasible, these efforts could be replicated and incorporated into the planning and priorities of DOW leadership. 6.1 Energy Resource and Technology Planning Although DERs can enhance grid reliability and resilience, the shift toward advanced energy technologies for installation-based energy requires additional engineering planning to manage daily resource supply. Traditional methods of long-term and short-term energy planning as well as real-time operations must evolve to address uncertainties surrounding resource availability and variability. The introduction of both variable resources and alternative generation resources increases system complexities, largely controlled by software. AI might be one tool to better manage generation resources. For example, DOE has identified opportunities for AI to inform grid management, including planning, permitting, operations, reliability, and resilience (Benes, Porterfield, and Yang 2024). AI support might involve power grid models, permitting assistance, and smart grids. Installing cyber-secure bidirectional charging equipment so that EVs can provide backup power to facilities would enhance resilience. For mission-based mobile energy technology planning and more advanced capabilities that are still under development, strategies to select suitable options and manage technologies could include custom cost-benefit analyses to identify trade-offs.
